common_name: Rotundiloba Fruitless Sweetgum (Seedless Round-Lobed Sweetgum with No Gumballs)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; Rotundiloba produces no seed balls, avoiding the spiny gumball litter of standard sweetgum on lawns and walkways.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; Rotundiloba is a naturally occurring seedless selection of American sweetgum, prized for producing the species' spectacular multicolored fall foliage display of yellow, orange, red, and burgundy-purple without the spiny seed balls that make standard sweetgum a nuisance on lawns, patios, and walkways. Its distinctive rounded, scalloped leaf lobes (rather than the pointed star shape of typical sweetgum) also make it easy to identify at a glance even before fall color develops. Like the species it grows into a large, handsome shade tree with a somewhat narrower, more upright habit than seed-grown sweetgum, transplanting readily when young and establishing quickly in the landscape. Because it sets no seed, it also does not provide the winter seed-ball forage that goldfinches and other birds rely on from wild sweetgum, a worthwhile tradeoff to weigh where wildlife value is a priority.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; beech resents root disturbance and compacted soil, so choose a permanent site with plenty of room to grow.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade, choosing a permanent location since beech roots are shallow and easily damaged by digging or soil compaction nearby. Copper Beech is a classic purple-leaved selection of European beech, prized for foliage that emerges deep purple-bronze in spring and generally holds a rich copper-purple color through summer before turning bronze-gold in fall, providing dramatic color contrast as a specimen or shade tree. It grows into a large, dense, majestic tree with smooth gray bark that stays attractive through winter, and its lower branches sweep gracefully toward the ground if left unpruned, though it can also be limbed up for a more traditional shade-tree form. It is a slow to moderate grower that rewards patience with great longevity, but it needs a real winter chill and struggles with the heat and humidity of the Deep South, performing best in cooler temperate climates well outside zone 9.

common_name: Princeton Sentry Ginkgo (Narrow Columnar Seedless Male Ginkgo)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Princeton Sentry is a grafted male clone selected specifically for a narrow, upright form and reliable seedlessness, making it a popular street and formal landscape tree.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; ginkgo tolerates urban conditions, air pollution, and compacted soil better than almost any other large landscape tree, making it a favorite for street and parking-lot plantings. Princeton Sentry is a male ginkgo selection prized for a distinctly narrow, upright, columnar form that fits streets and tight urban spaces where a full-spreading ginkgo would be impractical, while still developing the species' brilliant, uniform golden-yellow fall color that drops in a dramatic, near-simultaneous leaf fall. As a male clone it never produces the malodorous, messy fruit of female ginkgo trees, avoiding the notorious smell and slip hazard those seeds cause on walkways. Slow-growing and exceptionally long-lived, ginkgo is essentially pest- and disease-free once established, needing only a deep, infrequent watering during extended drought and no routine maintenance beyond structural pruning while young to establish a strong central leader.
